analysis.title: The Red Thread: Disruption 2.0 (2026 edition)
key_insights: AI is a macro-structural shock that makes traditional risk models (value-at-risk, historical stress tests, correlation matrices) less reliable. The authors move the problem from measurable risk to Knightian uncertainty and compare AI to electrification in the 1890s and the commercial internet in the 1990s.

Diversification by asset-class label can hide shared exposure to one AI build-out pathway. A portfolio of utilities, logistics real estate, semiconductor equities and IG credit tied to tech capex can load on the same driver.

Correlations between asset classes, such as the negative bond-equity correlation and commodity diversification, were conditional on a macro regime. They may strengthen, weaken or disappear as AI changes the economic pathways beneath them.

Ray Fuller proposes three diagnostic questions: pathway exposure to different AI outcomes, factor and linkage exposure across asset classes, and concentration under stress when a shared narrative or funding source is challenged.

The response to uncertainty is robustness, not forecasting precision. Fuller recommends the total portfolio approach (TPA), which measures risk units instead of allocation units and builds pre-mortem protocols, while noting it still depends on the judgment of the user.

Macro (Brown and Khan): geopolitics is now a persistent driver of macro regimes through three channels: energy security, supply-chain rewiring and reserve/fiscal regime shifts. Energy security may command a new premium, and globalization is being rewired, not dismantled.

Macro: reserve diversification into gold, real assets and non-dollar arrangements is a marginal shift. The USD stays dominant, but defense, energy and industrial spending add fiscal strain, so sovereign balance sheets, term premia and currency dynamics matter more. Argentina and Venezuela are named as places where markets may be slow to adjust.

Jeffrey Ding interview: AI leadership is decided by diffusion across the wider economy, not by who innovates first. He favors tracking talent flows and token usage and discounts survey data (for example '90% of businesses use AI'). He sees the US as better positioned than China, but notes US limits on talent flows and higher-education funding as a risk.

Ding sees a real chance that ultra-large-scale AI capex will not pay off near term for the companies spending it, comparable to the dot-com cycle, while long-run productivity gains still arrive. He also flags a high-profile AI accident as a possible brake on diffusion.

Ian McIntosh (UBS AM head of AI) says LLMs work best as a sparring partner, not an assistant. He warns that models optimize for plausibility, can hide errors behind fluent output, and are most useful to people who least need them. Experience and verification gain value, and he expects investment workflows to change visibly within three years.

Credit: the roughly USD 35B Apollo/Blackstone private-credit deal (June 2026) funded an SPV that bought about a million Google custom AI chips and leased them to Anthropic. Broadcom supports the senior notes and Google backstops site leases. Anthropic added about 1GW of compute with no debt on its own balance sheet.

Credit: consensus hyperscaler capex is near USD 940B in 2026 and USD 1.3T in 2027. Net hyperscaler IG issuance is about USD 274B year to date versus USD 130B in 2025 and USD 40B in 2022. Datacenter-specific issuance exceeds USD 169B. Supply has been a spread headwind.

Credit: UBS estimates aggregate hyperscaler obligations rise from about USD 800B to roughly USD 3.5T once off-balance-sheet commitments are included. The authors say the clearest credit risks lead back to the AI research labs, which are unprofitable and compete intensely at the model layer.

Credit: evidence points to a compute shortage, not a glut. Resale contracts are short-dated and priced at a premium. The authors say consensus capex estimates have likely caught up to reality, but spread levels remain tight.

Credit: Oracle was cut to BBB- (stable) by S&P on 9 July 2026. Its remaining performance obligations rose to USD 638B from USD 138B a year earlier, much of it from OpenAI. US high-yield technology trades about 40bp wider than the index, after being nearly 100bp wider.

Credit positioning: UBS sees value in strategic data center debt with low energy risk and good construction records, and in higher-yielding compute-linked bonds. It would avoid issuers funding long-lived infrastructure with short-lived technology and thin protection, or with heavy single-counterparty exposure.

Equity/value (Magill): the authors take a deliberately contrarian view that AI reshapes software value pools rather than eliminating software demand. Verticalized, deeply embedded SaaS with proprietary data and high switching costs may be mispriced as permanent decline.

Equity/value: avoiding structurally disrupted franchises is the primary discipline. They look cheap and cash-generative while ROIC erodes. The team favors less crowded enablers, such as specialized semiconductors for mobile and IoT, over richly valued, crowded infrastructure winners.

Infrastructure (Muir): electricity is the binding constraint, with long interconnection queues and transformer lead times. US data centers used about 4% of national electricity in 2023 and are projected at 7% to 12% by 2028. UBS puts cumulative AI capex near USD 4.7T for 2026-2030.

Infrastructure: value may sit in contracted power, transmission and transformers, electrifying commodities, and digital infrastructure with assured power and permits. Orbital compute is best viewed as long-dated optionality, a call option on launch costs, not an allocation.

Infrastructure: labor displacement is likely concentrated in language- and code-intensive white-collar tasks, with first pressure in entry-level hiring. Litigation such as Mobley v. Workday targets AI vendors as well as employers, and EU AI Act high-risk obligations are delayed to December 2027.

sector_views.rationale: Industry-specific, deeply embedded software with proprietary data and high switching costs may be priced as permanently impaired when AI is likely to enhance it.
Visible infrastructure winners trade at very high multiples with crowded positioning. The team prefers less obvious enabling segments.

sector_views.sector: Power, grid equipment and electrification commodities
sector_views.rationale: Contracted, reliable power and long-lead grid equipment are the binding constraint on AI build-out.
Headline revenue can look stable while ROIC deteriorates, and these value traps form faster than in most areas.
Fundamentals are strong, but heavy issuance and off-balance-sheet obligations leave spreads tight. UBS sees selective value in strategic datacenter debt.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Consensus has been revised up more than once. UBS thinks estimates have likely caught up to reality.
Shows the scale of financing needed, which pushes capital markets to the center of the build-out.
Too large to fund from company balance sheets alone.

trade_ideas.description: Selective long in strategic data center debt with low energy risk and reputable construction histories
trade_ideas.rationale: Tight compute supply and take-or-pay contracts, prepayments and guarantees support the downside.
trade_ideas.risk: Duration, counterparty and technology risk remain, along with regulatory and construction risk.

trade_ideas.description: Long higher-yielding bonds tied to compute that outperform if pricing stays tighter than the market expects
trade_ideas.rationale: Scarce high-end compute strengthens operators at contract renewal.
trade_ideas.risk: Today's compute pricing cannot be underwritten forever, and capacity could rise as new sites come online.

trade_ideas.description: Long vertical-market SaaS companies with proprietary data and embedded workflows that add AI as an enhancement
trade_ideas.rationale: Switching costs are high and the market may be pricing AI disruption as permanent decline.
trade_ideas.risk: Disruption risk is real but uneven, and a large margin of safety is needed.

trade_ideas.description: Hold orbital compute only as long-dated optionality, a call option on launch costs collapsing, not as an allocation
trade_ideas.rationale: Orbital hardware still faces power cost, heat rejection and maintenance obstacles.
trade_ideas.risk: Power in orbit costs far more than terrestrial solar or gas, and the launch rocket is still in testing.

risk_factors: Narrative-driven concentration: holdings that look diversified share one AI disruption pathway.
Correlation matrix instability makes backward-looking risk models unreliable.
AI research labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) are unprofitable and weak credits, and a lab that fails to scale profitably could hit leveraged cloud and data center debt.
Off-balance-sheet opacity: hyperscaler obligations rise from about USD 800B to USD 3.5T once off-balance-sheet commitments are included, and private labs hide more debt.
Circular financing and counterparty concentration, with a single guarantor (Broadcom) behind tens of billions in chip-lease debt.
Residual value risk on chip leases if in-house silicon shifts market shares.
Electricity, interconnection and transformer constraints, and community and water pushback.
Reversal in AI capex, or a high-profile AI accident that erodes public trust.
Software disruption and value traps in high-yield software capital structures built for lower rates.
Labor displacement, which could weaken consumer demand and force fiscal support.
Regulatory and litigation exposure, including vendor liability under Mobley v. Workday and EU AI Act timing.
charts_described: Figure 1 plots hyperscaler capex for IBM, META, ORCL, GOOG, AMZN, MSFT, CRWV and SPCX from 2020 to 2028, using Bloomberg consensus estimates from August 2026.

Figure 3 shows hyperscaler obligations adjusted for leases not yet commenced, service commitments, production commitments, and backstops and guarantees, less cash, with the total near USD 3.5 trillion.
vol_and_positioning: Crowded positioning in highly visible AI infrastructure winners leaves these stocks at very high multiples.
US high-yield technology spreads are about 40bp wider than the index, after being nearly 100bp wider. European spreads have largely retraced January's widening.
Spreads and market caps of US software issuers such as Salesforce and Adobe have seen volatility spikes while cash flow stays robust.
geopolitical: Renewed concerns around Middle Eastern supply routes returned energy security to the center of the macro narrative.
Europe's effort to reduce dependence on Russian gas is cited as an example of rapid energy repricing.
US-China technology competition: US export and talent restrictions versus China's active management of technology companies.
Sanctions and financial restrictions are encouraging sovereign reserve diversification into gold, real assets and non-dollar arrangements.
SpaceX's filing for a constellation of up to a million satellites as orbital data centers, with Google, Amazon, Nvidia-backed Starcloud and China's space program pursuing similar ideas.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers have strong balance sheets, real cash flows and visible demand in cloud revenue, contracted backlogs and a compute shortage. Resale contracts are short-dated and priced at a premium, and take-or-pay contracts, prepayments and guarantees firm up the downside.
tension_points.bear_case: Off-balance-sheet obligations of about USD 3.5T, circular financing, weak lab credits (OpenAI, Anthropic) and uncertain useful lives of financed chips. Debt of cloud operators would be exposed if a lab failed to scale profitably.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A research lab failing to scale profitably, a closing of the financing window, or an imminent break in model scaling laws.

tension_points.bull_case: Software with proprietary datasets and systems of record in regulated or complex industries is hard to displace, and AI features can add revenue or improve retention.
tension_points.bear_case: Structurally disrupted franchises look cheap and stable while ROIC deteriorates, and value traps form faster than in most areas.
tension_points.what_invalidates: ROIC erosion, falling reinvestment rates and pricing power in a franchise that screens as cheap.

tension_points.bull_case: As with the internet, computing infrastructure ultimately transformed productivity, and AI will take a growing share of the energy budget with broad productivity gains.
tension_points.bear_case: Capex in ultra-large-scale clusters may not pay off near term for the companies making it, and the US-Japan computing history includes the dot-com crash.

theme_stances.key_argument: Asset-class labels hide shared exposure to the same AI disruption pathway, so correlation-matrix diversification is unreliable.
theme_stances.evidence: The first casualty of AI-era uncertainty is traditional diversification.

theme_stances.key_argument: Backdrop is constructive and cautionary: supply is tight and structures protect the downside, but obligations are opaque and the labs are weak credits.
theme_stances.evidence: For creditors the backdrop is constructive as much as cautionary.

theme_stances.key_argument: Embedded vertical SaaS with proprietary data may be mispriced as permanent decline.
